newsitem.title: USA: U.S. in effort to end air restrictions with Asia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. in effort to end air restrictions with Asia.

text.p: Officials from the United States and Singapore held a final day of talks Wednesday toward reaching an "open skies" aviation agreement, part of a wider U.S. effort to end air services curbs throughout Asia.
A Transportation Department official said the two-day Washington talks followed an informal meeting last October in Singapore, which included South Korea, Taiwan, Malaysia and Brunei.
There was no immediate report on any progress made in the talks with Singapore, but the official said further meetings were planned, although a date had not yet been set.
The United States held exploratory talks with Japan, its major Asian aviation partner, on Jan. 10-11, and is to hold further talks at an unspecified future time.
Liberalised aviation agreements, although not "open skies" accords, are already in effect with India and Thailand.

Major U.S.-Singapore routes are now flown by United Airlines, a unit of Chicago-based UAL Corp., and Singapore Airlines Ltd., but an "open skies" agreement would allow additional carriers to start competing services.

U.S. attention turned to Asia last year after a series of "open skies" agreements were reached with Canada, Germany and a number of smaller European countries. Talks are also being held with Britain, but so far with little apparent progress.
Earlier, free market agreements were reached with the Netherlands and Canada, paving the way for increased flights.

The Clinton Adminstration's aim to end curbs on flights to Asia, to the benefit of American carriers, is based on airline passenger travel estimates that in the next 10 years traffic to Asia will exceed that to Europe.
But the Japanese market has proved difficult to open.
The United States has argued that the world is turning toward ending restrictions on aviation services and that countries that resist could be left behind.

Japanese officials have argued that their existing accord with the United States was weighted in favour of the United States and an "open skies" pact would only increase the dominance of the U.S. mega-carriers.

U.S. officials say the aim behind writing separate "open skies" agreements with the smaller European nations, as well as Germany, was to press Britain into negotiations to keep up as as continental European markets opened.

The officials hope that the talks with Singapore and later talks with other smaller Asian nations would do the same with Japan -- press it to negotiate out of fear it would be left out of the growing trans-Pacific market.

They say that if free market accords are written with the smaller Asian nations, but not Japan, U.S. carriers would no longer fly through Japan to other Asian points, but bypass it to serve the area's smaller but faster-growing economies.
